stances.claim: With the Court's new composition (seven of the eight QW majority retired), it is time to restore the constitutional shroud that justices be removed only by impeachment and only on the grounds clearly provided -- Republic v. Sereno should be reopened at the first available opportunity.

Jardeleza's Gios-Samar deflection misses the substantive issue; ample jurisprudence exempts cases of transcendental importance from the 'paralysis of procedural niceties,' and the Court's independence is of the highest transcendental importance to the nation.

The Sereno decision was 'harsh' on three asymmetries: same-day eviction before MR period lapsed (criminals get 15 days); expunction from the list of CJs and exclusion from the Gallery (impeached Corona was kept in the Gallery); and denial of retirement benefits despite a 6-year tenure (longer than predecessors and all successors).

The 'self-inflicted sword of Damocles' over incoming justices -- risk of QW removal by present and future administrations -- is unjust, unethical, and unwise; the question of whether to keep dangling it is for the Court itself.
stances.rhetorical_move: rhetorical-question catalog (just/ethical/wise) inviting reflection rather than answer

stances.claim: Three further questions deserve reflection: (a) whether justices who testified at the House impeachment proceedings should have voted in the QW case; (b) whether the eight should have accepted posts/benefits created by their own acts and votes; (c) whether dissenter Carpio's decision to decline the CJ post created by the decision he opposed reflects the more honorable answer.

CJ's own posture is disinterest: he stands to gain nothing whether the Court upholds his views or not, and would respectfully decline any post or benefit if offered -- his only aim is restoring SC independence.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-disinterest disclosure to authorize the critique

notable_anecdotes: Jardeleza's parade of post-QW positions (4 became CJ, 1 Ombudsman, 1 GSIS chair-and-former-CJ, 1 JBC member) recited 'with a hint of pride' -- and CJ's pointed refusal to comment on those gains: 'I will refrain from commenting on the posts and benefits they reached or gained after ousting their chief.'

The same-day eviction of Sereno before the MR period lapsed -- paired with the criminal-procedure comparator: 'Even hardened criminals convicted of the most despicable crimes are allowed 15 days to file their MRs before their judgments became executory.'

The Corona-vs-Sereno asymmetry -- Corona, constitutionally impeached and removed, was included in the Gallery of CJs and eventually granted retirement benefits; Sereno, ousted by QW, was expunged and denied -- turning Gallery inclusion into the silent comparator of institutional generosity.
The 2009 leaked-decision-justice case -- penalties 'lifted' by 2014, no immediate eviction, full 15-day MR -- used as the elephant-in-the-room counterfoil to Sereno's treatment.
Carpio's principled decline of the CJ nomination created by a decision he dissented from -- surfaced as the honorable benchmark against which the eight's post-QW acceptances are implicitly measured.
Closing quartet of 'is it just, ethical, and wise' questions -- designed to be answered not now but by history; the rare CJ column that explicitly defers its own judgment to time.

one_paragraph_summary: Replying to retired Justice Francis H. Jardeleza's May 8 commentary defending the Republic v. Sereno (May 18, 2018) QW decision, Panganiban restates his April 8 position: with the Court's new composition (seven of the eight QW majority have retired), it is time to restore the constitutional shroud that justices be removed only by impeachment, and only on the grounds clearly provided. He notes Jardeleza's parade of post-QW positions (four became CJ, one is Ombudsman, another GSIS chair, another a JBC member) 'with a hint of pride' -- and pointedly refrains from commenting on the posts and benefits gained after ousting their chief. He answers Jardeleza's procedural-bar deflection (Gios-Samar v. DOTC) by invoking the transcendental-importance exemption from the 'paralysis of procedural niceties' -- the Court's independence is of the highest transcendental importance to the nation. He explains why the decision was 'harsh': it was immediately executory, evicting Sereno before the MR period lapsed though even hardened criminals get 15 days; she was expunged from the list of CJs, stripped of the first-woman-CJ honor, and her picture excluded from the Gallery; she was denied retirement benefits despite a 6-year tenure longer than all her successors -- while in 2009 a justice found guilty of leaking a decision was given his 15-day MR and his penalties eventually lifted, and impeached CJ Corona was kept in the Gallery and granted benefits. CJ leaves the reversal question to the new Court but poses four 'just, ethical, and wise' questions for reflection: continuing to dangle the 'self-inflicted sword of Damocles' over incoming justices; the participation of justices who had testified at the House impeachment proceedings; the eight's acceptance of posts and benefits their own votes created; and Senior Justice Carpio's honorable decline of the CJ post created despite his dissent. 'Let us pause and reflect. And let history be the judge.'
